intro:
The Ice March

February 23rd, 1918

Rostov is ours. The Volunteer Army left in the dark and has gone off the railway into open steppe, where our armoured trains cannot follow.

Nobody is chasing it into the snow. Take the Don crossings behind it instead - Rostov, Aksaiskaya, Ol'ginskaya - so that nothing of theirs can turn back on the city. Let four of their formations get clear and the Kuban gets an army.

briliant.text:
Rostov, Aksaiskaya and Ol'ginskaya are in Soviet hands and the lower Don is shut. The task the Committee set me has been carried out.

The column itself is gone into the Kuban. I will not pretend otherwise, and I will not write in my report that we destroyed it: we had neither the cavalry nor the fodder to hold open steppe in February, and no one who has seen that country in a thaw would promise it. What we have done is take away its base. Kornilov marches now with what he carries, and every stanitsa behind him belongs to the Soviets.

They will be back. Whatever they gather in the Kuban, they will have to come back through these same crossings, and we shall be standing on them.

That is the whole of it. The Kuban will now have to fight the battle we should have finished on the Don.

intro:
Tragedy at Ekaterinodar

April 9th, 1918

Kornilov has six thousand men and no base. There are three times that in Ekaterinodar, and he will attack anyway, because he can attack or starve on the steppe.

He will not try the front of the city: a crossing is being prepared to the west, at Elizabetinskaya. Hold both faces and take Takhtamukay across the river, where his column forms up.

briliant.text:
Ekaterinodar has held. On the fourth morning of the assault a shell came through the wall of the farmhouse at Elizabetinskaya where Kornilov had his headquarters, and killed him where he stood. Denikin took over what was left and broke off the attack that night.

They buried him somewhere on the road and ploughed the ground over the grave so we would not find it. We found it.

Their army is not destroyed - it is going back to the Don, where Krasnov's Cossacks have risen and the German divisions in Ukraine will sell them anything they can pay for. But the Kuban is Soviet, and the man they called the soul of the whole affair is dead.

intro:
Belaya Glina

June 28th, 1918

Denikin is back in the Kuban with nine thousand men, German rifles bought through Krasnov, and the whole Don behind him. Torgovaya has gone and the Tsaritsyn railway is cut.

Nothing is coming from the north: Moscow has the Germans in the Ukraine and the Czechoslovak revolt on the Volga. Hold Belaya Glina, Novopokrovskaya and Peschanokopskoye - while we sit on those junctions this army still has a spine.

briliant.text:
The three junctions are still ours and their forward depot is a field of burnt tarpaulins. General Markov was killed by one of our shells at Shablievka a few days back, and the Officers' Regiment that carries his name went into our wire twice today and came out thinner both times.

The task was to keep the line open, and the line is open. Further south, though, Tikhoretskaya is being turned, and an army that cannot be told what to do by wire cannot hold a front three hundred versts wide. We are going to have to shorten it.

intro:
The battle for Ekaterinodar

August 13th, 1918

Tikhoretskaya has gone and Denikin has brought up everything he has for the capital of the Kuban. Half the stanitsas have gone over to him.

His recruiting is also his weakness: behind him the land goes back to its 1916 owner, the ataman returns, and the punitive detachment explains it to the village - and those villages recruit for us. Hold Ekaterinodar and the western crossing; clear Plastunovskaya, where his staff sits.

briliant.text:
The line held and Plastunovskaya is ours, with a staff car, a printing press and four sacks of their correspondence in the bargain.

It changes less than it should. Novorossiysk and the coast road are already lost, the railway to the north is cut in three places, and an army supplied by nothing but peasant carts cannot sit in a city with sixty thousand mouths in it. The Army Council has decided to go to Armavir and fight for the Terek instead. We leave in good order, on our own feet, with our guns - which after this summer is not nothing.

I have burned nothing and shot no one on the way out. Let them find the city as they find it, and let the people of Ekaterinodar compare.

intro:
The Taman Army

August 23rd, 1918

The Taman group is cut off by two hundred versts of White cavalry, sea on one flank and mountains on the other, with thirty thousand people on the road and a rifle for one in three.

Kovtyukh has one route - the coast road east through Gelendzhik - and German warships to keep him out of the harbour. The order is four words long: get the columns out. Not the ground, not the guns.

briliant.text:
Eight columns are through Gelendzhik and on the coast road, and the rearguard came out in order behind them with its machine guns still mounted.

The town is lost. It was lost before we started; a port under naval guns with no fleet of our own was never going to be held, and I said so at the council. What was in our hands was whether the Taman Army came out as an army or as a crowd on a road, and it has come out as an army.

They have five hundred versts of mountain track ahead of them to reach Armavir, and they will do it on foot, in August, eating what the stanitsas give them. When the history of this war is written that march will be in it.

intro:
Stavropol

November 10th, 1918

Denikin has drawn a ring round this army from three sides and is pressing it back on the mountains. Stavropol has changed hands twice, and both times cost whole regiments.

We are the 11th Army on paper, which has improved nothing, and the typhus takes more of us than the shelling. Hold Stavropol and the villages covering the road out of it. Wrangel is coming from the west, Drozdovsky from the north.

briliant.text:
Stavropol is held, both battery positions are taken, and Drozdovsky was carried off the field with a wound that the doctors say he will not survive.

The 11th Army is still an army. That was the whole of my task and it is done.

It does not lift the ring. The Terek is being rolled up behind us and the typhus is taking more men than the Volunteers are; a front cannot be held by a garrison that cannot stand up. What we have bought is time and an intact road eastward, and both will be needed.

intro:
Grozny

February 1st, 1919

The Great War ended in November, the Germans are gone from the Ukraine, and the Entente has begun unloading at Novorossiysk for Denikin: rifles, shells, instructors. Wrangel is at Vladikavkaz.

The Terek is the last thing we hold south of the Don and it is going a stanitsa at a time. Hold Grozny, Shali and Samashki - behind them there is nothing but the passes.

briliant.text:
The three towns are ours and their cavalry has been pushed off the river.

The 12th Army will still have to go over the passes. That was decided in Moscow and by the typhus, not here: with Vladikavkaz gone there is no front left to anchor on, and men who hold a town in an army that no longer exists are simply prisoners who have not been taken yet. We come out with our formations intact and our wounded with us.

The oil wells are burning again. We did not fire them; the retreating administration did, in 1918, and the Volunteers will say it was us. Let them.

intro:
The Manych

May 1st, 1919

The 10th Army put itself across the Manych in the winter and for a few weeks the southern front looked like splitting in two. Wrangel has brought his Caucasus corps up by rail with British armour.

This steppe belongs to whoever has the most horses, which is not us, so it comes down to the crossings. Hold Velikoknyazheskaya, Uyutnyy and Ekaterinovka; Torgovaya, taken in the winter and lost again, is worth having back.

briliant.text:
The fords are held and Torgovaya is ours again, with their forward dumps in it.

The 10th Army will nonetheless be pulling back over the Manych within the month. Not because of anything that happened on this ground: the Don Cossacks have risen behind our left at Veshenskaya, the 9th Army's flank has gone, and a bridgehead is only as good as the army standing behind it. We go back over the river as a formation, in our own time, with the crossings still in our hands - which is the difference between a withdrawal and a rout.

intro:
Tsaritsyn

June 14th, 1919

The Cossacks have come at this town three times and gone back three times with nothing, which is why the papers call it the Red Verdun. The workers' regiments, the armoured trains and the gunboats are all still here.

What is different is Wrangel, the tanks the British landed for him, and our own front north of here coming apart since the Veshenskaya rising. Hold Tsaritsyn, its approaches and the river crossing; clear their heavy batteries off Gorodistsje.

briliant.text:
The city is held, the crossing is open, and the battery position at Gorodistsje has been overrun with its guns still limbered.

The town will not stay ours for long, and everyone in this headquarters knows it. Denikin has issued what he is pleased to call the Moscow Directive; the whole southern front is moving, and Tsaritsyn is one anchor on a line that has already been turned in three other places. When we go, we will go with the army intact, the shops emptied and the barges upriver, and the men who held here will be needed at Orel.

There is a phrase going round the staff about the defence of last autumn - about the commissar from Moscow who requisitioned everything on the Volga and shot the specialists who argued. I have no orders to repeat it and no wish to. What held Tsaritsyn was the trenches and the men in them.

intro:
Oboyan

August 12th, 1919

Denikin's Moscow Directive is three armies on three axes for one capital. May-Mayevsky is coming up the Kharkov railway to deliver the middle of it, and Mamontov's cavalry is already in our rear areas.

The 13th Army is to hold the Oboyan-Pristen line long enough for the reserves forming at Orel and Tula to be worth something. That is a screen, and everyone has been careful to call it something else. Break their group at Yakovlevo and buy three weeks.

briliant.text:
The line held for the whole of the allotted time and Yakovlevo was cleared on the last day. The reserves at Orel have their three weeks.

Kursk will still have to be given up. That is the army's decision and it is the right one: a screen that stays in place until it is surrounded has stopped being a screen. We go back on the Oboyan road in our own order, and the divisions that come out of here will be in the line at Orel when it matters.

One warning from the army: replacements will not be reaching us for some weeks. Count your losses before you take them.

The reserves at Orel will have to form up with the enemy already in front of them.

intro:
Peregonovka

September 26th, 1919

Makhno's people have retreated west across half the Ukraine for a month with Slashchev driving them. This morning the whole Insurgent Army turned round in the dark and went at the pursuit head-on.

There is a great deal between us politically and there will be a reckoning. Tonight that is not the point: the group at Peregonovka is Denikin's, it sits astride the railway to his rear while his front line reaches for Orel, and it can be destroyed.

briliant.text:
The pursuit group has been broken and ridden down. The tachankas came in across the stubble at first light and there was nowhere for the column to form square.

What follows matters more than the field. Denikin's rear in Ukraine is open, his supply trains from Berdyansk and Mariupol have to be found from somewhere else, and every regiment he sends back to deal with the insurgents is a regiment not marching on Moscow.

I have written up the action honestly, including who did the riding. There will be people at the front headquarters who will not want to read it that way.

I am to rejoin the Southern Front. Nothing has been taken off the enemy's back and the whole weight of it is now coming north.

intro:
Orel: the avalanche

October 11th, 1919

Kutepov is coming up the Moscow highway with the Kornilov, Markov, Drozdovsky and Alekseyev regiments - officers with nothing left to go home to, and nobody has stopped them this summer.

We are not asked to stop them either. Hold Orel, Mtsensk, Kromy and Dmitrovsk long enough for the shock group forming behind Kromy - the Latvian riflemen, the Estonians, Primakov's Chervonny Cossacks - to come into line unspent.

briliant.text:
We held the line to the hour we were given, and the shock group at Kromy has come up complete: eleven thousand bayonets that have not yet been in this battle.

The high command has decided not to fight for the city itself with the troops already worn out on this ground. Orel may be given up for a few days if the shock group is thereby put in on the flank instead of being fed into the front. That is not a defeat of ours; it is what the last week was bought for.

Latyshi are already moving into position west of Kromy. The counterstroke goes in this week.

Kutepov is on the Tula road. What is left of this army is going back with him behind it.

intro:
Orel: the storm

October 16th, 1919

Five days ago their newspapers printed the distance from Orel to Moscow. They were right about the distance and wrong about everything else.

That corps has fought eleven weeks without a reserve on a widening front; Makhno is across its supply line, and its regiments are officers, who cannot be replaced out of villages it has just requisitioned. The shock group goes in at Kromy, where its line of retreat runs. Take Orel back.

briliant.text:
Orel is ours. Kromy is ours. The Kornilov regiment left its wounded in the school at Dmitrovsk and went south in the dark.

This is the turn of the whole war and it should be written down as such while the ground is still warm. From here the Southern Front does not defend; it advances. Kursk, then Kharkov, then the Donbass, and then the sea.

The Latvian regiments lost heavily in the wood north of Kromy. Their commander asked that the divisional order should name the companies rather than the division. It will.

intro:
Tula

November 3rd, 1919

Tula makes the rifles. That sentence is the whole of the situation. Their advanced parties are at Plavsk, thirty versts down the road.

Against them: the workers' regiments of the arms works, a fortified belt the townspeople dug themselves through October, and six divisions freed from Voronezh and Tsaritsyn - which the enemy made possible by concentrating everything here and leaving his own left flank in the air. Hold the belt.

briliant.text:
The belt held and the arms works never stopped. Sixty thousand rifles went out of this town while the fighting was inside artillery range of it.

That is the end of their northern effort. Their left has been stripped bare to make this attack and Budyonny's cavalry is already through the gap at Kastornoye. We are going back onto the Kharkov line - forward, at last, and on our own initiative.

The belt was forced south-east of the town. The works are being evacuated by rail under fire and the machinery that cannot be moved is being broken up.

The road north is open. There is one line left in front of Moscow and we are it.

intro:
Moscow

December 12th, 1919

Their cavalry is in the outer suburbs. The Council of Defence has not left, the Kremlin garrison is in the line, and the barricades were thrown up by people carrying their own tools.

Hold the three southern sectors and Red Square. Volkhonka on the Kaluga road is where their staff and heavy batteries have come up; take it and the attack loses its hinge. There is no line behind this one, which simplifies the orders.

briliant.text:
The city is held. The attack has stopped at the barricades and gone no further, and this morning their forward regiments were seen going back down the Kaluga road with their guns.

They cannot stay where they are. Their army is four hundred versts from a railhead it still holds, in December, with the Don rising behind it and the Ukrainian rear in insurgent hands. What broke here was not just an assault but the whole idea of the march on Moscow.

The front headquarters wants me back in the south for the pursuit. I am to go by the first train.

I am ordered north tonight, to Petrograd, where the last formed reserve of the Republic is. I do not want to go and I am going.

intro:
Petrograd

January 26th, 1920

This sector is detached to the 7th Army, and the opponent is no longer Denikin but Yudenich - the North-Western Army, armed out of Reval, with British tanks and naval guns off Kronstadt.

Petrograd has been stripped for every other front for two years; what is left is the workers' regiments, the sailors and the courses cadets. Hold the city sectors and the airfield - their road in, and their road out, runs through the Moscow highway junction.

briliant.text:
The city is held and the North-Western Army has come apart in front of it. Their formations are going back over the Estonian border to be disarmed and interned by the government they were fighting for.

It is over on this front, and it ended the way this whole war seems to end things: not with a surrender but with an army walking off the map. Peace talks with Estonia begin at Tartu within days.

I am recalled to the Southern Front. Kharkov is the next name in my orders.

intro:
Kharkov

December 4th, 1919

Since Orel this front has not stopped. Kursk went in November, Budyonny is cutting the Donets railway in three places, and the army that was to be in Moscow by Christmas cannot man its own line.

It is also finding out what its rear is worth: the districts it requisitioned all summer send it no recruits. Kharkov is the hinge - take the three city sectors and the Donbass position goes with them. Be quick; their rearguard is fighting for days, not ground.

briliant.text:
Kharkov is ours with its workshops, its rolling stock and eleven locomotives that were still under steam. Their rearguard did not have the time it wanted.

Their army is splitting in two: one part towards Rostov and the Kuban, the other towards the Crimea. Once that has happened it cannot be undone, and neither half can support the other. The pursuit goes on to the sea.

We took the city, but slowly, and slow was the one thing that mattered here. Their rearguard held the crossings the extra four days it needed and their staff and depots are out along the Rostov line.

They will be able to reform on the Don. We shall have to fight for that too.

intro:
Novorossiysk

March 12th, 1920

The Kuban has gone, Rostov has gone, Ekaterinodar went last week, and everything left of them is trying to get into the last port they hold on this coast.

In the roadstead are British and French warships and nothing like enough transports; their command has listed who is taken off, and the men who are not have worked that out for themselves. Take the Novorossiysk port, or break up the evacuation columns at the moles.

briliant.text:
The port is ours. What was still on the quays when our cavalry came down the hill went into captivity where it stood - twenty-two thousand men, the horses, the guns, and the stores the ships had no room for.

Part of the army got away to the Crimea. That was decided in the roadstead by the tonnage available and not on this ground. What did not get away was the Armed Forces of South Russia as a field army; Denikin resigned command within the fortnight.

Wrangel has taken over what reached Sevastopol. There is one more campaign in this.

The embarkation went on to the end and the transports sailed full. We came down to a quay of abandoned horses and burning stores.

Everything that got onto those ships will be facing us again in the Crimea, and it will have British guns when it does.

intro:
Perekop

November 7th, 1920

Wrangel has spent a summer turning the isthmus into a fortress - the Turkish Wall, the Yushun positions, eight belts of wire, every gun the French landed. He has said publicly that it cannot be taken.

So it will not be taken the way he built it to be taken. The front attacks frontally while the Sivash, which this wind makes fordable, is crossed the same night. Take Armyansk and the wall, then Krasnoperekopsk and Zalivnaye behind it.

briliant.text:
The Wall is taken and the Yushun positions behind it are taken. The columns that went across the Sivash came out of the mud on the far shore at four in the morning, into the flank of the whole position, and after that the fortress that could not be taken was a line of concrete with nobody behind it.

Wrangel is embarking at Sevastopol, Yalta and Feodosiya. He is doing it well - better than Novorossiysk, and there are ships for everyone who reaches the quays. A hundred and fifty thousand people are leaving Russia and most of them will not come back.

The war in the south is over. I am forty-one years old, I have served two Russias, and I am going to write to Katya that she can come home.
